title: Zitong’s complete component list
notes: Zitong’s entire original slide is preserved without rewriting or cropping: FPGA and package, LEDs, reference clock, flash, inventory statements, comparison parts and the source boot-validation caveat. Inventory figures are dated source statements. Pan and zoom to discuss individual entries. Zitong's source calls XC7A35T-2CSG325I the final FPGA decision. Its requirements are XC7A series, at least two GTP lanes, more than 120 user I/Os, more than 100 units in stock, authorized AMD distributors and the smallest suitable package. It reports 122 units at JLCPCB and says packages smaller than 15 × 15 mm do not provide enough I/Os for this design. These are Zitong's dated selection claims, rather than current purchasing verification. M1 retains this FPGA and both indicators. The eight-chip statement describes the intended system, rather than demonstrated operation. This slide preserves Zitong's proposed clock list and order. The source says Jiaao confirmed that one oscillator can serve the FPGA and GTP clock domains. The oscillator is described as 3.2 × 2.5 mm, ±25 ppm and 186 fs RMS phase jitter typical. The splitter is described as 1:2 LVDS, 1.8 V, up to 2 GHz and VQFN-16 at 3 × 3 mm. Review comments belong here: the source asks for better than ±20 ppm while listing ±25 ppm, and RMS phase jitter does not establish its <10 ps peak-to-peak cycle-to-cycle jitter request. The reported oscillator characterization uses 3.3 V rather than M1's selected 1.8 V. The typed LMK1D2102LRGTR suffix differs from the source's linked LMK1D2102RGTR. M1 adopts the oscillator and AC coupling, but provisionally omits the LMK while the GTP ODIV2 fabric-clock route awaits Vivado verification. Listing the LMK here records Zitong's proposal, rather than claiming it is fitted in M1. This slide preserves Zitong's flash section and programming workflow. Its requirements are small size, a single SPI interface, Vivado recognition and Artix-7 support. The source gives the ISSI flash a 1.65–1.95 V supply and up to 166 MHz operation. It gives the NXP translator 1.08–1.95 V A-side, 1.65–3.6 V B-side, up to 208 MHz and XQFN-16 at 2.6 × 1.8 mm. Reported inventory and future distributor arrival dates are dated source claims and stay out of the slide body. The source explicitly says NVT4858 was designed for SD/SDIO and that FPGA boot/configuration behavior still needs validation. M1 adopts these exact parts with SPI x1, adapted idle biases and separate boot holds. Physical boot and brownout behavior remain open. The displayed programming path is the source's intended workflow, rather than a completed software demonstration.

title: FPGA PCB schematic
notes: Native M1 two-sheet schematic, unchanged. Select either sheet, then pan and zoom. Gerald’s guidance is to match related clock/data, review bypass, returns and manufacturable escapes. This is a schematic-checked direct-interface prototype; routing, clock implementation, sequencing and hardware validation remain open. The October 6 feedback highlighted routing quality, regular placement and unmatched delays. The earlier directions also call for power-distribution checks, practical blind-via escapes, compact placement and bottom connectors. Our engineering application is to review the full signal and return path, not only visual symmetry. A factory stackup and guaranteed ASIC timing still need evidence. Our next concrete review should use the native two-sheet FPGA drawing and the new carrier PCB. The requirements that still need ASIC-side evidence are pad levels, recording data-valid timing, rail currents and power-loss behavior. The fabrication stackup and mechanical seating need supplier or physical evidence. The one-chip XEM path is the first integration step, with eight-chip scaling following verified results.
sources: FPGA35T_M1.kicad_sch and ASIC_Signals.kicad_sch, native KiCad SVG exports

title: Existing ASIC LDO board
notes: Show the LDO and carrier sides of each connector pair. J1 provides the defined LDO circuit interface. J19 remains a required physical mating point even though its source contacts are electrically unassigned. The native pad positions register in plan; final connector seating and board clearance are still to be confirmed against populated hardware and supplier mechanical data. The original J19 has 24 signal-pad positions and four additional numbered end pads. The end-pad function and numbering remain to be confirmed; 28 CAD pads should not be described as 28 electrical connector contacts. This is Gerald’s existing LDO design. Its 23 digital signals pass directly between the connectors. The rail intents include separate nominal 1.5 V domains, 1.6 V, 0.75 V and two high-stage circuits. The high-stage sign and reference must stay explicit. All nine LDO power-good outputs are unused in the saved circuit, so a raw-input monitor does not establish that every ASIC rail is ready. Actual fitted parts, currents, return bonding and power order remain to be checked. The new Desktop package contains the connector-foundation carrier. Show where the LDO and XEM sockets sit and how the recording bus runs between them. Do not call this a complete powered carrier. The older R3 and R5 circuits remain different revisions, and the R3 manufacturing hold remains in place. The received board uses two copper layers and has no ground plane. The saved Step 8 uses four copper layers and a dedicated In1.Cu DGND plane. Select top, underside, J1 or J19 on the left. Select the carrier or LDO 3D on the right. Source generic bodies and missing connector housings do not qualify physical seating.
